Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

title: ACO Seminar: Alexander Polyanskii (Emory University) (Thursday, October 1, 2026)
text:
ACO Seminar: Alexander Polyanskii (Emory University) takes place on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Wean Hall 8220.
Event: ACO Seminar: Alexander Polyanskii (Emory University)
Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:00 PM to 4:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 8220
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Speaker: Alexander Polyanskii , Emory University

Tight colorful no-dimensional Tverberg theorem

Abstract: In this talk, I will discuss a tight colorful dimension-free Tverberg theorem. If P1,…,Pk are finite disjoint sets of n points in a Euclidean space, then our result guarantees a partition of the union P1∪⋯∪Pk into n rainbow sets of size k such that a single ball intersects the convex hull of every set. The radius of this ball depends only on the number of color classes, the number of rainbow sets, and the largest diameter of a color class — not on the dimension of the ambient space. Moreover, the resulting bound is best possible.

The key tool is a Pythagorean-type subadditivity property of the Chebyshev radius, which is of independent interest. Given sequences X=(x1,…,xn) and Y=(y1,…,yn) of points in a Euclidean space, contained in balls of radii RX and RY, respectively, one can re-enumerate Y so that the pointwise-sum sequence Z=X+Y is contained in a ball of radius satisfying R2Z≤R2X+R2Y.

This is joint work with Polina Barabanshchikova and Grigory Ivanov.

title: Distinguished Speaker Series: Roozbeh Kiani (Thursday, October 1, 2026)
text:
Distinguished Speaker Series: Roozbeh Kiani takes place on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Mellon Institute (MCS) 328.
Event: Distinguished Speaker Series: Roozbeh Kiani
Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:30 PM
Venue: Mellon Institute (MCS) 328
Organizer: Neuroscience Institute
Description: Dr. Roozbeh Kiani
Professor, Neural Science and Psychology, New York University

Thursday, October 1, 2026
3:30 PM
Mellon Institute: Room 328

Summary: Flexible behavior requires flexible decision-making. We adapt seamlessly to changing environments—adjusting biases, altering decision rules, and inferring hidden task contexts—often without explicit cues. In this talk, I will outline a framework that formalizes different levels of this flexibility and show how these adjustments are implemented in neural codes across the frontoparietal cortex. I will highlight three forms of decision flexibility: (1) Bias adjustments, driven by asymmetric rewards, shift neural activity along the decision variable axis; (2) Rule changes, such as varying sensory weights in a multi-feature discrimination task, produce rotational changes in the population geometry, supporting rapid changes in decision policy; and (3) Hierarchical inference, where animals infer hidden contexts to adapt to task structure, is reflected in the emergence of latent variables represented in distributed subspaces.

Venue: Virtual - Registration Required
Organizer: Civil and Environmental Engineering Department
Description: “Co-creating tomorrow: Community Driven Engineering for a Resilient Future” is a webinar series exploring the critical intersection of community wisdom and engineering expertise in the face of a changing climate. Organized by CERCA, CMU CEE’s Center for Engineering Resilience and Climate Adaptation, this series will foster a deeper understanding of how community engagement can enhance the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of climate adaptation initiatives.

This semester, the series will focus on community-driven engineering for coastal adaptation. Drawing on real-world experience, speakers will shed light on what coastal adaptation looks like in practice - examining how communities approach sea-level rise, how engineers fit into the collaborative process, and what it truly takes to build lasting resilience together.

As director of The Water Institute’s Community Resilience Center, Renee draws from on-the-ground experience working in underserved communities and navigating federal, state, and local governmental processes and systems to help support effective and equitable climate resilience planning and action in communities across the Gulf Coast.

Registration is Required.

title: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Emily Leiner (Illinois Institute of Technology) (Friday, October 2, 2026)
text:
Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Emily Leiner (Illinois Institute of Technology) takes place on Friday, October 2, 2026 at 11:00 AM at 3941 O’Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA - Allen Hall - 321.
Event: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Emily Leiner (Illinois Institute of Technology)
Date: Friday, October 2, 2026 at 11:00 AM
Venue: 3941 O’Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA - Allen Hall - 321
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Emily Leiner (Illinois Institute of Technology)

Title: The Rotational Fingerprints of Post-Mass-Transfer Binaries

Abstract: Mass transfer in binary systems creates a variety of important astronomical objects, including Type Ia supernovae and other transients now being discovered in time domain surveys. Yet many fundamental parameters governing mass transfer physics are still not well understood, including the criteria for mass transfer stability, angular momentum evolution, and the efficiency of mass transfer. In this talk I will focus on rotation as a diagnostic of recent mass transfer. I will discuss the rotational evolution of accreting stars, and demonstrate some new methods to detect post-mass-transfer populations that utilize the wealth of rotational data coming from TESS and other all-sky time domain surveys. I will further discuss a new approach to measuring masses and ages of post-mass-transfer stars in open clusters using the Bayesian code BASE-9. Combining these mass and age constraints with rotational information can yield critical new constraints on mass transfer stability and efficiency. Together, these results show that rotation is a largely untapped tool for discovering and characterizing a broad population of post-interaction binaries.

Description: Abstract: This presentation reviews recent advances in Microsoft’s Majorana-based topological qubit program, highlighting progress in materials, device architecture, and qubit measurements. Results demonstrate improved topological energy scales, enhanced parity stability, and scalable tetron-based qubit arrays enabled bysuperconductor-semiconductor nanowire technology. These developments represent important steps toward fault-tolerant quantum computing with topologicalqubits.

Michael Nystrom earned his B.S. in Metallurgical Engineering and Materials Science from Carnegie Mellon University and a Ph.D. in Materials Science and Engineering from Northwestern University, where he studied nonlinear optical properties of ferroelectric thin films. He spent 20 years in Silicon Valley working on the fabrication and assembly of optical devices for applications including displays, telecommunications, and mobile imaging. At Microsoft, he contributed to the development of the HoloLens augmented reality headset, leading MEMS scanning mirror technologies, and now works in the Quantum program focusing on packaging and integration of quantum devices in cryogenic environments.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Saturday, October 3, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Saturday, October 3, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. (Reading Room & Exhibitions)

Talk Title: The Policy–Practice Gap in Privacy: Why Legal Protections Fall Short and How to Make Them More Effective

Abstract: Around the world, data protection and privacy laws are proliferating as policymakers seek to protect consumers from harms arising in a data ecosystem fueled by the extensive collection, use, and sale of personal information. Yet these laws often fail to produce meaningful improvements in consumers’ privacy in practice.

Dr. Schaub’s research investigates how public policy and legal requirements affect consumers’ privacy in practice. His empirical findings show that privacy notices rarely provide meaningful transparency into companies’ data practices; cookie banners do not support informed consent; despite the availability of privacy rights and controls, consumers often permit more data collection and third-party sharing than they expect; and effective identity-theft protections, such as credit freezes, continue to have low adoption rates.

In this talk, Dr. Schaub will discuss his group’s empirical research on these issues and identify factors that create and sustain the privacy policy–practice gap. Description: Speaker: Natalia Perkins (University of Minnesota)

Title: Probing Fractionalized Excitations in Kitaev Spin Liquids.

Abstract: Quantum spin liquids are highly entangled states of matter in which conventional magnetic order is avoided even at very low temperatures. A particularly important example is the Kitaev spin liquid, which provides a rare exactly solvable setting where interactions between localized spins give rise to emergent fractionalized excitations. At the same time, Kitaev physics is believed to be relevant to a growing family of candidate quantum materials, making it possible to search experimentally for signatures of these exotic excitations. Establishing such signatures in real materials, however, remains a major challenge.

In this colloquium, I will discuss several ways in which the fractionalized excitations of Kitaev spin liquids can be probed experimentally. I will focus in particular on lattice vibrations, which provide a natural window into the magnetic sector through spin-phonon coupling, and discuss how signatures of fractionalization can appear in phonon dynamics and Raman spectroscopy. I will also discuss local probes, including tunneling spectroscopy, and the perhaps counterintuitive role of disorder: vacancies and other defects need not simply obscure spin-liquid physics, but can generate characteristic local excitations and provide additional probes of the underlying fractionalized state.

Description: Abstract: Modern AI systems are increasingly built by placing trained models inside larger computational loops. Inference-time algorithms are a basic instance of this idea: they use one or more trained models at test time to incorporate new information, exploit pretrained models as priors, and trade computational effort for accuracy, sample quality, or control. Examples include generator-verifier search for reasoning, diffusion models for solving inverse problems, and reward-guided generation. Theoretically, this revisits a classical question from optimization and theoretical computer science: what can be done with access to an oracle? Here, however, the oracles are new and non-standard: they model the capabilities of large pretrained models, making them powerful, but also imperfect because they are learned. This combination leads to new questions about algorithm design and error propagation.

This talk studies two central aspects of this paradigm: computational efficiency and error propagation. The first vignette considers generator-verifier systems, and shows how stochastic backtracking can trade additional computation for accuracy, giving a principled version of test-time scaling even with imperfect learned oracles. Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

Description: Instruction can be difficult for both teachers and students following a major incident or tragedy. These events may take an emotional and cognitive toll on students, disrupt their lives, and interfere with learning for extended periods of time. Students’ proximity to such an event does not always determine their response. For example, students may be seriously affected by incidents that involve total strangers. Additionally, students’ surface responses may not be indicative of the actual effect.

As an instructor, it’s important to consider the impacts such events have on students as human beings and learners. In this seminar, we will discuss considerations for determining whether or not to address an event in the classroom and develop multiple strategies for addressing distressing events in your classes.

Venue: Wean Hall, 7316
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Michal Papaj (University of Houston)

Title: Pair density modulation in iron-based superconductors

Abstract: Pair density modulation (PDM) is a phenomenon recently observed in exfoliated flakes of iron-based superconductors [1], in which the superconducting gap oscillates strongly with the same periodicity as the underlying crystalline lattice. In this talk, I will present the current experimental evidence of PDM and discuss a model [2] that explains this modulation in systems with broken nonsymmorphic symmetries through the emergence of nematic superconductivity, which further breaks the four-fold rotation symmetry. This results in a sublattice texture on the Fermi surface, aligned with the anisotropic superconducting gap of the nematic s+d state. This gives rise to distinctive gap maxima and minima located on the two inequivalent iron sublattices while still being a zero-momentum pairing state. I will discuss how further investigation of such modulations can give insight into the nature of the superconducting pairing, such as the signs of the order parameters and visualization of a phase transition to a mixed two-component state using local probes.
[1] L. Kong, MP, H. Kim, Y. Zhang, E. Baum, H. Li, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, G. Gu, P. A. Lee, S. Nadj-Perge, Nature 640, 55-61 (2025)
[2] MP, L. Kong, S. Nadj-Perge, P. A. Lee, Nature Communications 17, 7480 (2026)

Description: Over the past 30 years, the online advertising industry built a large-scale data collection ecosystem, with the goal of tracking a user’s online activity to infer their demographics and interests. Traditionally, the ecosystem relied upon the collation and analysis of highly-structured text data like user IP addresses, GPS coordinates, e-commerce purchase histories, and visited URLs. However, recent ML models can parse not only structured text, but also multimedia files and unstructured text inputs — meaning a user’s photos, videos, inboxes, and calendars are now ripe for automated analysis. The privacy risks are particularly acute in the context of smartphone apps. A user’s phone already acts as a natural collation point for sensitive user information, but users may not understand that permitting an app to, for example, access a user’s photo does not just give the app access to the bytes in the photo: the app also receives access to inferences about the user that are enabled by the photo.

Priva-See, an LLM-based inference system for app-collected user data, was built to explore these privacy risks; Priva-See reflects our best understanding of how real-life adtech companies would leverage machine learning to build user profiles. Through an IRB-approved user study, 465 participants deployed Priva-See on their phones; Priva-See made privacy-invasive inferences despite having access to only a subset of a user’s data. Description: Artificial Intelligence has become the central arena of US-China strategic competition, but the public debate — fixated on which country’s frontier model tops the latest benchmark — misses where the contest is actually being decided. This talk maps the layers that matter: compute and semiconductor supply chains, the export control regime and its mounting unintended consequences, and the industrial ecosystems that determine who deploys AI at scale. It examines how China’s AI sector has adapted under US restrictions — the surge of open-weight Chinese models in global adoption, Huawei’s advanced packaging workarounds, and Beijing’s countermoves on critical materials and state-directed capital. For policymakers, the uncomfortable finding is that several US controls are producing the opposite of their intended effects: accelerating Chinese substitution, eroding the market position of allied firms, and ceding influence over the global AI stack. The talk closes with the emerging third dimension of the relationship: AI safety and governance. In the wake of the first US-China dialogue on frontier model governance, it assesses whether Beijing’s rapidly maturing domestic safety-evaluation infrastructure represents a genuine basis for cooperation, a bid for standards-setting influence, or both — and what a realistic agenda for engagement looks like when the two countries are simultaneously racing and talking. Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

Title: What makes your point particle a black hole

Abstract: Worldline quantum field theory (WQFT) efficiently adapts QFT
techniques to classical dynamics, enabling the calculation of the
two-body problem in GR to unprecedented precision in the
post-Minkowskian expansion. In this talk, I will present recent
developments in the WQFT description of rotating compact bodies,
summarize the basics of WQFT perturbation theory, and highlight the need
for higher-dimensional operators … because black holes are not point
particles! Identifying the operators relevant to black hole dynamics
requires matching to black-hole perturbation theory (BHPT). I will
present ongoing work establishing the connection between WQFT and BHPT,
including in the presence of spin, with the goal of determining an EFT
for Kerr black holes beyond linear order in curvature.

text:
Departmental Seminar: Dr. Ankur Jain takes place on Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room.
Event: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Ankur Jain
Date: Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 1:40 PM
Venue: Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room
Organizer: Biological Sciences Department
Description: Guest Speaker: Ankur Jain, PhD

Associate Professor of Biology at MIT

Core Member, Whitehead Institute

Title: Keeping RNA in Shape: Folding, Misfolding, and Aggregation in Cells

Our lab studies how RNA folds, misfolds, and aggregates in cells. RNA readily self-associates in a test tube, yet most cellular transcripts remain soluble. In this talk, I will discuss how this balance can break down in repeat-expansion disorders. We find that the sequences surrounding a repeat and aberrant splicing can alter where repeat-containing RNAs accumulate and lead to unexpected protein products, suggesting possible routes to neurological disease. I will then turn to the broader question of how cells limit aggregation across the transcriptome. Combining experiments and simulations, we find that native mRNA sequences are unusually resistant to self-association: folding within individual molecules helps limit intermolecular interactions and aggregation. These findings suggest that maintaining transcriptome solubility constrains genome evolution.

Departmental Hosts: Professors McManus and Zhang

Price: Free
Description: In an era of environmental reckoning and social unrest, architectural practice and pedagogy must cultivate a community-centered discipline that serves as a bold experiment, a tangible demonstration, and a new common.

Addressing the critical intersections of the climate crisis, social equity, and food apartheid, The Urban Classroom: Sankofa Bamboo Greenhouse establishes a design-build methodology anchored in material adaptation and reuse, digital prefabrication and empirical structural verification. Winner of ACSA 2026 Best Design Project.

Located in Pittsburgh’s Homewood neighborhood, the project provides vital spatial infrastructure — including a sapling nursey, a gathering space, and weekend market platform – for the Sankofa Village Community Garden , directly confronting the persistence of local food insecurity while empowering the urban community it serves. Through a full-scale design-build intervention in an underserved neighborhood, it constructs a compelling case for low-carbon practice, framed as an act of community solidarity and sustainable intervention. At its core, the project is dedicated to expanding the boundaries of both professional practice and architectural education while producing exemplary instances of community-driven architecture.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Thursday, October 8, 2026 at Posner Center.

Date: Thursday, October 8, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

title: CERCA Virtual Guest Lecture with Dr. Xinyue Ye (Thursday, October 8, 2026)
text:
CERCA Virtual Guest Lecture with Dr. Xinyue Ye takes place on Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 11:00 AM at Zoom - Registration Required.
Event: CERCA Virtual Guest Lecture with Dr. Xinyue Ye
Date: Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM
Venue: Zoom - Registration Required
Organizer: Civil and Environmental Engineering Department
Description: Title : From Digital Twins to Autonomous Intelligence: GeoAI for ResilientCities and Infrastructure

Abstract: Cities and infrastructure are complex spatial systems shaped by interactions among the built environment, human activities, mobility, and environmental processes. Drawing on a series of our studies using university campuses as living laboratories and microcosms of cities, this talk traces the evolution from GeoAI-enabled digital twins toward autonomous spatial intelligence. I will show how heterogeneous geospatial and human activity data can be integrated to represent physical and social systems, optimize spatial decisions, predict changing conditions and human behaviors, and incorporate spatial knowledge and constraints into AI reasoning. These studies demonstrate how digital twins can evolve from representations of the real world into dynamic systems that connect sensing, prediction, simulation, reasoning, and feedback. Building on this foundation, I will discuss how emerging multimodal and agentic AI can further enable digital twins to continuously sense, learn, reason, and support action, pointing toward autonomous intelligence for more resilient cities and infrastructure.

title: AI-SDM Seminar Series (Harvard Session): Tomer Ullman (Thursday, October 8, 2026)
text:
AI-SDM Seminar Series (Harvard Session): Tomer Ullman takes place on Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 12:00 PM at 3.301 Science Engineering Complex (SEC), Harvard University.
Event: AI-SDM Seminar Series (Harvard Session): Tomer Ullman
Date: Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:30 PM
Venue: 3.301 Science Engineering Complex (SEC), Harvard University
Category: Career & Professional Development, Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: AI-SDM
Description: Abstract When we imagine things, many of us have the impression that we create full, rich, vivid scenes. But, we also have the impression of a full, rich world before us in perception, and decades of cognitive science have proven us wrong. I’ll examine how recent work shows that when we imagine, we may only be creating partial scenes, leaving parts of the scene uncommitted, with much of the work of the imagination done by rough-and-ready representations.

Speaker Bio
Tomer Ullman is a cognitive scientist interested in common-sense reasoning, and building computational models for explaining high-level cognitive processes and the acquisition of new knowledge by children and adults. In particular, he is focused on how children and adults come to form intuitive theories of agents and objects, and providing both a functional and algorithmic account of how these theories are learned. Such an account would go a long way towards explaining the basics cogs and springs of human intelligence, and support the building of more human-like artificial intelligence. Dr. Ullman received in B.Sc in Cognitive Science and Physics from Hebrew University in 2008, and his Ph.D. in Brain and Cognitive Sciences from MIT in 2015. From 2015-2018 he was a post-doctoral associate at the Center for Brains, Minds, and Machines.

Description: Join Carnegie Mellon University faculty experts Emily DeJeu and Chris McComb (ENG 2014, 20216), alongside Ashish Kapur (TPR 1996), Global Leader for Data, Artificial Intelligence, and Industry Solutions at AWS Professional Services, for a timely conversation exploring how humans and AI can work together to create greater value than either could alone. Drawing on research, teaching, and real-world business applications, the panel will examine how AI is changing learning, communication, innovation, and leadership across industries.

How AI is reshaping the skills professionals need to succeed

What effective human-AI collaboration looks like in practice

The future of communication, creativity, and decision-making

What business leaders should be doing today to prepare for tomorrow

Date: Friday, October 9, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Description: Speaker: Lina Necib (MIT)

Title: Dancing in the Dark: Data, Models, and the Milky Way’s Dark Matter

Abstract: In this talk, I will explore the interfacing of simulations, observations, and machine learning techniques to construct a detailed map of dark matter in the Milky Way, and argue that progress now hinges on the dance between the information content of our data and the fidelity of our models. For the Galactic halo, I will present recent work leveraging Gaia DR3 that reveals a declining stellar rotation curve. I will then show how underestimated errors can bias the resulting curve, and how we used simulations to build a more robust error treatment that reconciles the measurement with other probes of the Galaxy’s enclosed mass. In dwarf galaxies, stellar data of the faintest systems will not substantially grow and therefore I present GraphNPE, a graph neural network methodology that accurately extracts dark matter density profiles from sparse stellar kinematics. With GraphNPE, we find a hint of a core in Boötes I, consistent with predictions of self-interacting dark matter. Finally, I will invert the question and quantify, using mutual information, how the memory of the Milky Way’s merger history is progressively erased from stellar dynamics, setting a fundamental limit on what Galactic archaeology can recover. Description: North documents a new era marked by shifts in population that are transforming everything from the physical landscape of cities to electoral politics. With fast-moving markets and slow-moving governments, everyday people are caught in the crosshairs. While some will seek to preserve the status quo, others will relocate from places that are increasingly uninhabitable, too risky, or too expensive for permanent settlement. title: Soft Materials Initiative Seminar (Friday, October 9, 2026)
text:
Soft Materials Initiative Seminar takes place on Friday, October 9, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Scott Hall (6142).
Event: Soft Materials Initiative Seminar
Date: Friday, October 9, 2026 at 3:00 PM
Venue: Scott Hall (6142)
Organizer: Materials Science and Engineering Department
Description: Living pharmacy implants use engineered cells to synthesize and release therapeutic proteins on demand, offering closed-loop treatment of chronic diseases without repeated injections. Reaching clinically relevant doses requires dense cell encapsulation, but these cells consume oxygen faster than passive diffusion can supply it. Existing oxygen sources either deplete rapidly or lack release control. In this talk, we present WireOx, an implantable device that generates oxygen on demand by catalyzing water oxidation at sputtered iridium oxide films on platinum wire, with output precisely tuned by applied current.

We will show that controlled oxygenation sustains cell viability in high-density grafts and outline our progress toward in vivo validation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that controlled oxygen levels can actuate cell output through an oxygen-responsive genetic circuit within a narrow window bounded by hypoxic and hyperoxic stress. Finally, we will discuss the implications of this therapeutic window for designing oxygen-managed living pharmacy implants.

Category: Arts & Performance, Off Campus
Organizer: Carnegie Mellon University Press
Description: Reading: Begins at 7:00 PM

Opener: Layle Chambers

Reader: John Hoppenthaler

John Hoppenthaler is the author of four books of poetry: Night Wing over Metropolitan Area (2023), Domestic Garden (2015), Anticipate the Coming Reservoir (2008), and Lives of Water (2003). His work has appeared in numerous journals, anthologies, and textbooks. He is a professor of Creative Writing and Literature at East Carolina University, Greenville, NC.

Layle Keane Chambers is an author and poet whose work examines the intersection of landscape and lived reality, particularly of military families. She is the 2026 Elizabeth Boatwright Coker Fellow in Poetry, a finalist for the 2026 Colonel Darron L. Wright Memorial Writing Awards, and the VP of the Poetry Society of South Carolina. Holding Professor Emerita and an MFA in Poetry from New Mexico State University, her writing has appeared in Collateral, The Wrath-Bearing Tree, Line of Advance, and Proud To Be: Writing by American Warriors. Her debut chapbook Caught in the Light (Finishing Line Press) published in 2026, with the forthcoming BINGO ONE scheduled for July 2027. She is a proud Air Force mom.

Venue: CUC – Danforth Conference Room
Category: Career & Professional Development, Health & Wellness, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Office of the Vice Provost for Faculty
Description: This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

Event: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Regina Demina (University of Rochester)
Date: Monday, October 12, 2026 at 3:30 PM

Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Price: Free
Description: Speaker: Regina Demina (University of Rochester)

Title: Quantum observables at colliders

Abstract: The behavior of elementary particles is governed by quantum field theory, yet demonstrating their quantum nature experimentally is far from straightforward. Until recently, such demonstrations were either performed at relatively low energies or involved only composite particles. Recent results from the LHC have challenged this status quo by demonstrating entanglement in a system of the heaviest known fundamental particles—the top quarks.

A top-antitop quark pair produced at high energies constitutes a two-qubit system. The top quark has an extremely short lifetime of approximately 5 × 10−25 s, shorter than the characteristic hadronization timescale, 1/ΛQCD ≈ 10−24 s. Consequently, the top quark decays before hadronization, transferring its spin information to the angular distributions of its decay products. This unique feature has been exploited by both the ATLAS and CMS experiments to measure spin correlations between the top and antitop quarks. In certain regions of phase space, these correlations are strong enough to satisfy the Peres–Horodecki criterion for entanglement.

Near the threshold for top-antitop production, an enhancement of the spin correlations beyond theoretical predictions has been observed, pointing to the possible formation of a bound state, commonly referred to as toponium. Description: We welcome all to a series of discussions that address this year’s theme of “Shakespeare and Technology.” We will be interpreting the theme broadly, inviting papers on Shakespeare studies and performances in today’s technological landscape, as well as work that concentrates on technologies of the early modern period.

The conference is open to scholars at all levels, including graduate students for regular sessions and undergraduate students for roundtable seminars. Graduate students and undergraduate students have been encouraged to submit papers for the M. Rick Smith Memorial Prize and the Julia R. Lupton Graduate Prize.

We are pleased to be welcoming as speakers Alan B. Farmer (The Ohio State University), co-creator of DEEP: Database of Early English Playbooks, and Samuel Lemley (Carnegie Mellon University), Curator of Special Collections, CMU Libraries.

title: Distinguished Speaker Series: Pawan Sinha (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:
Distinguished Speaker Series: Pawan Sinha takes place on Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Mellon Institute Room 348.
Event: Distinguished Speaker Series: Pawan Sinha
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM
Venue: Mellon Institute Room 348
Organizer: Neuroscience Institute
Description: Of the estimated one million blind children worldwide, over 80% live in low- and middle-
income countries. For many, limited access to medical care results in years of unnecessary

blindness, even when their condition is surgically treatable. Project Prakash was founded to address
this humanitarian need while simultaneously pursuing a fundamental scientific question: How does
the human brain learn to see?
Through rural ophthalmic screening programs in India, Project Prakash identifies children with
treatable blindness and provides them with high-quality sight-restoring surgery at no cost to their
families. The onset of sight after years of congenital blindness creates a rare scientific opportunity -
by following these children longitudinally, we can investigate how the brain learns to extract
structure and meaning from visual information, whether and how different perceptual abilities
emerge, and how the potential for neural plasticity changes across development.
This talk will describe Project Prakash’s integration of medical service and scientific discovery and
present findings from behavioral, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging studies of children gaining
sight after prolonged blindness. These studies reveal both notable capacities for visual learning and
enduring consequences of early deprivation, providing insights into the mechanisms and limits of
human brain plasticity. More broadly, Project Prakash illustrates how addressing an urgent societal

title: CNA seminar: Tadele Mengesha (University of Tennessee) (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:
CNA seminar: Tadele Mengesha (University of Tennessee) takes place on Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 1:00 PM at Wean Hall 7218.
Event: CNA seminar: Tadele Mengesha (University of Tennessee)
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 1:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 7218
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Variational Convergence and Approximation of Parameterized Nonlocal Models

Abstract: I will discuss a class of parameterized linear nonlocal problems in which the parameter measures the degree of nonlocality. As this parameter varies, both the underlying function spaces and the corresponding solutions change, and the models may transition from nonlocal equations to a limiting local equation.

Focusing on scalar fractional equations and strongly coupled systems arising from bond-based peridynamics, we develop a variational framework for analyzing such parameter-dependent optimal design problems. We establish variational convergence and compactness results, resulting in a rigorous description of the behavior of solutions and the nonlocal-to-local transition.

We also introduce a numerical approximation framework that is consistent with the asymptotic structure of the problem. The method provides approximations for every parameter value and guarantees unconditional convergence, with respect to both modeling and discretization parameters, to the solution of the corresponding limiting problem.

This work is based on joint research with A. Salgado and J. Siktar.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections (Friday, October 16, 2026)
text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Friday, October 16, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Friday, October 16, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

text:

Event: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Karen Masters (Haverford College)
Date: Friday, October 16, 2026 at 11:00 AM
Venue: 3941 O’Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA - Allen Hall - 321
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Karen Masters (Haverford College)

Title: Spirals in Galaxies: Physics and Observations

Abstract: The iconic spiral arms that decorate the disks of massive galaxies (like our own Milky Way) have been studied observationally and theoretically since they were first recorded nearly 200 years ago, nevertheless the exact details of their physical nature remains elusive. I will review the basic physics of spiral galaxy dynamics, with an emphasis on what is known observationally about spiral arms, including results from the citizen science project Galaxy Zoo (www.galaxyzoo.org) and the large galaxy survey “MaNGA” (Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory - part of the SDSS). I will discuss how these and other observational data are currently being used to constrain the variety of different physical models which have been proposed to explain spiral arms in galaxies.

title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections (Sunday, October 18, 2026)
text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Sunday, October 18, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Sunday, October 18, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Monday, closed

Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. (Reading Room & Exhibitions)

Description: Speaker: Ruobo Zhou (Penn State University)

Title: Unraveling the nanoscale architecture and multifunctional roles of cytoskeletal scaffolds with super-resolution imaging

Abstract: Super-resolution fluorescence imaging has transformed our ability to visualize molecular organization at nanometer scales, yet imaging complex assemblies over extended timescales and across multiple protein species remains challenging. We recently developed FLEXTAG, a compact, self-renewable, anti-photobleaching protein-labeling platform enabling multiplexed and sustained super-resolution imaging. We applied these approaches to the neuronal membrane-associated periodic skeleton (MPS), a lattice-like cortical structure of actin, spectrin, and associated molecules that provides a powerful model for understanding how nanoscale organization shapes cellular function. Using co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry, we identified hundreds of candidate MPS-interacting proteins, and super-resolution imaging of representative examples — including previously unknown structural components, motor proteins, cell adhesion molecules (CAMs), ion channels, and signaling proteins — revealed periodic distributions characteristic of the MPS along neurites. Genetic perturbations indicate roles in axon–axon and axon–dendrite interactions and in axon diameter regulation. Functionally, the MPS serves as a dynamic platform for signal integration, recruiting G protein-coupled receptors, CAMs, and receptor tyrosine kina

text:

Organizer: Statistics & Data Science Department
Description: Abstract: Understanding the extent to which increases in atmospheric aridity are driven by temperature versus precipitation changes is important for informing adaptation efforts for crop stress and wildfire risk. Because controlled experiments on the global climate system are impossible, this is an observational causal inference question, complicated by the high dimension of the treatment field. To answer causal inference questions in climate science, we propose a spatio-temporal stochastic intervention framework with a conditional shift estimand and a regularized inverse probability weighting estimator with a tunable penalty parameter for balancing the bias-variance tradeoff. We show through simulation studies that this estimator outperforms alternative IPW-based estimators at recovering the true causal effect, and correctly adjusts for the confounding bias incurred by an unadjusted estimator. Applying this framework to the estimation of the causal effect of temperature on aridity, adjusted for precipitation, in climate-model simulations, we show that the effect of historical warming on vapor-pressure deficit emerges in the mid-1990s, and that an unadjusted estimator inflates the global estimate by nearly half. Venue: Wean Hall 8220
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Fluctuation of the structure of random walk ranges

Abstract: We investigate fluctuation phenomena for the graph distance and the effective resistance associated with random media arising from the range of a random walk. The behavior of such objects plays a central role in a variety of problems, including volume growth, metric scaling, and universality phenomena in random geometry. Our results demonstrate a sequence of dimension-dependent phase transitions in the scaling behavior of these fluctuations, leading to qualitatively different regimes across dimensions lower than six, equal to six, and higher than six.

This is joint work with Arka Adhikari and Daisuke Shiraishi.

title: Science Denialism through an Anti-Vaccination Lens: A Rhetorical Analysis of Online Multimodal Discourse (Monday, October 19, 2026)
text:
Science Denialism through an Anti-Vaccination Lens: A Rhetorical Analysis of Online Multimodal Discourse takes place on Monday, October 19, 2026 at 4:30 PM at McKenna Room, CUC.
Event: Science Denialism through an Anti-Vaccination Lens: A Rhetorical Analysis of Online Multimodal Discourse
Date: Monday, October 19, 2026 at 4:30 PM to 6:00 PM
Venue: McKenna Room, CUC
Organizer: Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences
Description: How does online opposition to vaccination become a critique of established sources of knowledge and authority? This presentation examines visual and verbal discourse about vaccination posted by geographically dispersed online groups between 2011 and 2020. A rhetorical analysis identifies four recurring frames: Anti-Capitalism, Back to Nature, Free Choice, and Surveillance, Oppression, and Deceit. The findings show how vaccine hesitancy can serve as an entry point for broader distrust towards modern cultural institutions, such as governments, the media, and science. They also reveal how posts combine frames and sustain ambiguity strategically, in ways that may appeal to different audiences. The project contributes to institutional theory more broadly by examining how multimodal rhetoric can erode institutional authority and the legitimacy of established knowledge.

Price: Free
Description: A native of Rehovot, Israel, Ilan Morgenstern is formerly the Bass Trombonist of the Vancouver Symphony, and in addition member of the San Antonio Symphony, Houston Grand Opera Orchestra, Jacksonville Symphony and Kansas City Symphony, Morgenstern has also performed with the Detroit Symphony, Philadelphia Orchestra, Atlanta Symphony, Dallas Symphony, Utah Symphony, Houston Symphony, Virginia Symphony, New Israeli Opera, and the Israel Philharmonic.

Morgenstern’s concerto performances have included engagements with the with the San Antonio Symphony, United States “Pershing’s Own” Army Orchestra, Millennium Orchestra (Seoul, Korea), Jeju Symphony Orchestra (Jeju, Korea), and the National Repertory Orchestra.

In addition, Morgenstern has won numerous awards for his playing including the Jeju International Brass and Percussion Competition, Zellmer-Minnesota Orchestra Competition, National Repertory Orchestra’s Concerto Competition, and is a recipient of the Lewis Van Haney Bass Trombone Philharmonic Prize.

Labeled a “must buy” in the International Trombone Association Journal, Morgenstern’s debut recording project It’s Alive!! New Music for Bass Trombone, a collaboration with composer Robert Denham and pianist David Gilliland was released in May of 2016.

Venue: Wean Hall 8220
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Project-based learning in Math Classroom

Abstract: Project-based learning (PBL) is a highly effective active learning strategy, yet integrating it into a standard mathematics curriculum presents unique structural challenges. Drawing on practices from multiple institutions and educational research, this seminar explores the end-to-end design of PBL components within a differential equations course. I will break down the course structure and project structure, examine the mechanics of project evaluation, the integration of computational tools and AI, and how these collaborative assignments interact with core theoretical material, and other active learning strategies. Through a demonstration of pedagogical practices and student feedback, attendees will leave with scalable materials and concrete strategies to develop PBL components in their own courses.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 8220.

Please complete this RSVP form if you plan on attending. Lunch will be provided to those attending in-person.

Category: Open to the Public
Organizer: Main Calendar
Description: An astonishing number of privacy and security issues are caused by people making bad decisions. An astonishing number of those decisions are accidents. This session examines how metric perversity and incentive misalignment drive poor decisions by rewarding activity instead of outcomes, turning measures into targets, and failing to account for uncertainty, black swans, and adversaries. Through practical approaches such as the Jerk Genie thought experiment, guard metrics, and uncertainty checks, the session presents a stronger framework for decision-making. The result is a model for building security and resilience through shared incentives and cross-functional integration across sales, finance, infrastructure, and product design.

Lea Kissner is LinkedIn’s Chief Information Security Officer, Vice President of Engineering and a prominent cybersecurity practitioner. They were at Google for 11 years, building much of the infrastructure security stack, co-inventing the Zanzibar access control system, and left as Global Lead of Privacy Technology – technical lead of all privacy engineering and responsible for approving every single launch across the company. After that they made a mark on some of the biggest firms in technology, including Zoom (security and privacy consultant), Twitter (starting as a Distinguished Engineer and Head of Privacy Engineering and becoming CISO and VP of Engineering), and then as CISO at cybersecurity startup Lacework. text:
Mathematical logic seminar: Grigory Terlov (UNC Chapel Hill) takes place on Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Wean Hall 8220.
Event: Mathematical logic seminar: Grigory Terlov (UNC Chapel Hill)
Date: Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 8220
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: pmp reductions in measurable combinatorics and percolation

Abstract: In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the measure class preserving (mcp) setting in measurable combinatorics. Surprisingly, generalizations to this setting have rarely relied directly on probability measure preserving (pmp) results. On the other hand, in percolation, a closely related field in probability theory, such reductions have been much more fruitful.

In this talk, I will explain a structural reason for this contrast and establish limitations on using pmp reductions to detect nonhyperfiniteness. On the positive side, I will show how weaker reductions can still be useful; for example, in constructing one-ended spanning subforests on mcp graphs. No prior familiarity with percolation theory or the mcp setting will be assumed.

This talk is based on joint work with A. Timar and an ongoing collaboration with M. Bowen.

Organizer: Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology
Price: Free
Description: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in national security, the most consequential challenges extend well beyond the performance of individual models. This talk will examine three interconnected priorities for national security AI: evaluating AI-enabled systems under operationally realistic conditions; evolving governance for rapidly evolving capabilities; and optimizing human-machine integration as AI becomes an increasingly important part of decision-making. Drawing on developments in AI decision-support systems, agentic AI, and embodied systems, the discussion will also examine emerging issues shaping the next phase of national security AI and consider AI as a social-cultural technology—one whose effects depend as much on people, culture, organizations, doctrine, and institutional incentives as on chips, data, models, and compute.
This dialogue will be moderated by CMIST Director Audrey Kurth Cronin. Virtual attendance option available. Please indicate how you plan to attend when registering.
Doors open at 4:30 p.m. ; refreshments served.

Description: Join us for an evening with artist RJ Messineo as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

About the Artist

RJ Messineo (born 1980, Hartford, CT; lives in Greenfield, MA) makes paintings involving observation and abstraction. In the last six years, Messineo has developed an idiosyncratic device for making paintings that involves attaching thin wooden boards to the surfaces of their canvases with magnets. Messineo received an MFA from the University of California, Los Angeles (2009) and a BFA from Cornell University, Ithaca, NY (2002). They have participated in exhibitions at Pace Gallery, New York; James Cohan Gallery, New York; Thomas Erben Gallery, New York; Ceysson & Bénétière, Koerich, Luxembourg; Night Gallery, Los Angeles; Artist Curated Projects, Los Angeles; Redling Fine Art, Los Angeles; and REDCAT, Los Angeles. Messineo is a Shandaken: Paint School Fellow and completed the Fire Island Artist Residency in 2014. Their work is held in the permanent collection of the Dallas Museum of Art.

Finding Kresge Theatre

Kresge Theatre is located in the College of Fine Arts building on the south end of CMU’s campus (near the Hunt Library). To find the theatre, enter the College of Fine Arts building from the west (main) entrance closest to the College of Fine Arts Lawn. Street parking is available along Frew and Tech streets or in CMU’s East Campus Garage.

Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

title: CMU Theory Seminar: Santiago Agui Salcedo (Chicago) (Wednesday, October 21, 2026)
text:
CMU Theory Seminar: Santiago Agui Salcedo (Chicago) takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Wean Hall, 8327.
Event: CMU Theory Seminar: Santiago Agui Salcedo (Chicago)
Date: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall, 8327
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Santiago Agui Salcedo (Chicago)

Title: Dissipative inflation in the CMB

Abstract:
There is an increasing interest in the interplay between Open Quantum Systems and Inflationary Physics. A time-dependent background and limited access to thedegrees of freedom invite the use of Open Quantum systems. It provides a more general framework than the unitary time evolution of a free state. In this talk, based on 2404.15416 and 2507.03103, we develop a local EFT for the scalar curvature perturbations subject to the dynamics of an open quantum system. We recover the scale-invariant power spectrum and then move on to the bispectrum. We study its amplitude and shape as a function of dissipation and other EFT parameters. Our results largely generalise the setup of warm inflation to general non-equilibrium cases. Finally, I will discuss the search for dissipative dynamics inthe CMB bispectrum and the current constraints on the dissipation scale from 2603.13473.

title: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Saket Navlakha (Wednesday, October 21, 2026)
text:
Departmental Seminar: Dr. Saket Navlakha takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room.
Event: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Saket Navlakha
Date: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 1:40 PM
Venue: Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room
Organizer: Biological Sciences Department
Description: Guest Speaker: Saket Navlakha, PhD

Associate Professor
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory

Title: “Algorithms in nature: from motor control to immune tolerance”

Biological processes can be viewed as algorithms that nature has evolved to solve problems that are important for survival. In this talk, I will describe two examples. The first is about the development of the neuromuscular circuit in the brain, which generates a unique architecture to facilitate movement using a “bipartite matching” algorithm. The second is about the development of the adaptive immune system, during which T cells learn to avoid attacking the body using a type of “generalization” algorithm. Both examples highlight my lab’s overarching goal of uncovering the algorithmic principles that underlie biological function.

Faculty Host : Professor Alison Barth

Description: Nathaniel Rosi University of Pittsburgh

Leveraging lability in MOFs: explorations in ligand exchange, interligand chemistry, and controlling compositional complexity

Host: Kevin Noonan

Wednesday, October 21st, 2026
4:00 p.m.
Mellon Institute Conference Room 348

Abstract: This presentation will detail ligand exchange phenomena and associated opportunities in classes of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) that contain either ligand bundles or multiple interconnected domains. Specific focus will be dedicated to explorations of how ligand bundling and ligand sterics influence ligand exchange outcomes and how consideration of these factors allows for systematic approaches to controlling ligand exchange. Finally, the presentation will detail how we are using this chemistry to control MOF compositional and structural complexity and to pursue new approaches for making molecules within the MOF milieu.

Bio: Nathaniel Rosi received a B.A. degree in chemistry in 1999 from Grinnell College and a Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of Michigan in 2003. After completing postdoctoral work at Northwestern University, he joined the faculty of the University of Pittsburgh as an Assistant Professor of Chemistry in 2006. He was promoted to Associate Professor of Chemistry with tenure in 2012, Professor of Chemistry in 2015, and Covestro Chair of Chemistry in 2022. He is currently serving as Department Chair. Description: The Screen Novel is an experimental form of digital storytelling that uses everyday digital interfaces—such as text messages, emails, notifications, maps, and social-media posts—as part of the narrative itself. Rather than simply illustrating a story, these fragments become the space through which characters, events, and emotions unfold.

In this introductory bilingual creative-writing workshop, participants will explore the possibilities of the Screen Novel through examples, discussion, and a guided writing exercise. The workshop will be presented bilingually in English and Arabic, and participants do not need to speak Arabic to attend.

No prior experience in digital design, programming, or creative writing is required.

Venue: MI 115
Organizer: Neuroscience Institute
Description: Active Perception in AR Displays

Trainee lunch and careers-in-industry discussion afterward

How should AR glasses work with a visual system that is constantly moving and making predictions? Scott will discuss how eye and head movements shape display design, from legibility and brightness to depth conflicts, flicker, and other visual artifacts. He’ll also cover how researchers simulate and test the visual experience before the hardware exists.

Description: Unlike conference assignment, which can be solved offline once all submissions are in, journal assignment must be done online: each paper assigned immediately upon arrival, from a pool of reviewers who may become unavailable for weeks once assigned.

We study this as an instance of online task assignment with reusable resources: tasks arrive over time, each must be immediately assigned to $k$ of $R$ available resources, and each assigned resource is busy for $d$ subsequent timesteps. This model captures peer review, healthcare scheduling, ridesharing, and emergency dispatch. I will present restless-bandit based policies and upper bounds. I will also discuss a closed-form Whittle index policy for automated reviewer assignment and insights from evaluation on a four-year trace of submissions to TMLR.

Led by students of all levels, these sessions offer a casual forum to discuss AI-related research while exploring cross-cutting connections between various disciplines in artificial intelligence. All students welcome!

Description: The SEI identified the seven areas because they have ongoing significance within cybersecurity’s rapidly evolving landscape, and each one represents operational and research focus that will drive significant improvements across a wide range of missions and systems. Description: Speaker: Pawel Pralat , Toronto Metropolitan University

Canonical labelling of random regular graphs

Abstract: We prove that whenever d=d(n)→∞ and n−d→∞ as n→∞, then with high probability for any non-trivial initial colouring, the colour refinement algorithm distinguishes all vertices of the random regular graph Gn,d. This, in particular, implies that with high probability Gn,d admits a canonical labelling computable in time O(min{nω,nd2+ndlogn}), where ω<2.372 is the matrix multiplication exponent.

Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Emmanuel Fonseca (WVU)

Title: Unveiling the “Fundamental Physics” Within and Around Binary Radio Pulsars

Abstract: The interplay of extreme gravity and nuclear astrophysics within neutron stars has led to an ongoing, century-long debate over the possible states of matter within their interiors. Multi-messenger measurements of neutron-star observables allow us to constrain their elusive “equation of state” (EoS), i.e., the statistical-mechanical relation that connects macroscopic parameters to the underlying microphysics. In this talk, I will describe how binary radio pulsars — rotating neutron stars that emit beamed radiation in orbit with other massive objects — will continue to provide influential measurements for probing aspects of “fundamental physics,” such as EoS physics and strong-field gravity. I will also discuss how forthcoming radio observatories will resolve nonlinear timing effects from Lense-Thirring precession in binary radio pulsars, likely allowing for a direct measurement of the neutron-star moment of inertia by 2040.

Speaker: Emmanuel Fonseca (WVU)

Description: ABSTRACT: Turbine disks that are used in oxygen-rich turbopumps for reusable rocket engines are subjected to centrifugal forces from high-speed rotation and rapid cyclic thermal transients. These loading conditions are challenging to mitigate in order to maximize thermal performance for engine efficiency while avoiding burst, fatigue, and frictional ignition failures. Typically, yield-limited design rules are used to avoid thermal fatigue failures while still maximizing allowable thermal gradients in the disk. In this study, alternative design rules are considered that leverage the plastic reserve while still safeguarding against burst and frictional ignition. In particular, both finite life design strategies and design rules based on the underused elastoplastic shakedown phenomenon are explored.

Dr. Natasha Vermaak is an Associate Professor of Mechanical Enginering and Mechanics at Lehigh University. She leads the Thermostructural Lab at the intersection of mechanics, materials, and design/optimization. Her group uses experimental and computational techniques to address problems of structural and material degradation, durability, and resilience. Her group applies optimization to design materials/structures at various scales. This includes the design and analysis of multifunctional architected materials and structures, especially in the inelastic and finite life domains. Event: Soft Materials Initiative Seminar
Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 3:00 PM
Venue: Scott Hall (Room 6142)
Organizer: Materials Science and Engineering Department
Description: ABSTRACT: Living systems are distinguished by dynamic and hierarchical assemblies of macromolecules far from equilibrium . My group studies phenomenon spanning the single-molecule to single-cell length scales, roughly 0.1 - 10 um, with the goal of controlling where biomolecules go and how they interact with each other . To do this, we develop new microfluidic techniques to manipulate biomolecules and cells with extraordinary precision and speed .

I will describe our active projects in this area, which include high throughput “cell surgery” by ultra-fast membrane stretching; biomolecular phase separation and self-assembly far from equilibrium; and biomolecular coacervates or ‘condensates’ as tools for engineering biology .

title: Colloquium: Hannah Rubin, Ph.D. (Friday, October 23, 2026)
text:
Colloquium: Hannah Rubin, Ph.D. takes place on Friday, October 23, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Baker Hall A36.
Event: Colloquium: Hannah Rubin, Ph.D.
Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 3:30 PM to 4:50 PM
Venue: Baker Hall A36
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Philosophy Department
Description: Citation gaps – systematic undercitation of women and minoritized scholars – are both an ethical and epistemic concern for scientific communities. We argue that these gaps emerge from field‑level norms about how much to read, how much to cite, and whether to prioritize relevance or prestige. We develop an agent-based model to analyze how these factors interact with demographic representation and homophily to create citation gaps. We also introduce an evolutionary model to examine how citation gaps change as representation increases over time and show that whether gaps diminish depends on a field’s relationship to the past: communities that weight recent work more heavily tend to see gaps shrink, while those anchored in canonical literature may sustain them even as representation grows. The analysis clarifies how local norms and long‑term dynamics jointly structure citation inequality.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Saturday, October 24, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Saturday, October 24, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

Category: Arts & Performance
Organizer: School of Music
Price: Free
Description: Praised by The New Yorker as “a fresh and vital young participant in what is a golden age of American string quartets,” the Daedalus Quartet has established itself as a leader among the new generation of string ensembles. Since winning the top prize in the Banff International String Quartet Competition, they have performed in many of the world’s leading musical venues including Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center, the Library of Congress, the Gardner Museum, and abroad at Vienna’s Musikverein, the Salzburg Mozarteum, the Concertgebouw, the Cité de la Musique in Paris, as well as in leading venues in Japan.

The Daedalus Quartet has won plaudits for its adventurous exploration of contemporary music including commissions of Fred Lerdahl’s Third String Quartet and Chaconne , Joan Tower’s White Water , Huck Hodge’s The Topography of Desire , David Horne’s Flight from the Labyrinth , and Vivian Fung’s Frenetic Memories.

Since 2006, the Daedalus Quartet has served as Quartet-in-Residence at the University of Pennsylvania where they are recognized for their innovative programming and interdisciplinary collaborations, particularly in their Beethoven Quartet cycle, Music and Migration, Hearing Women’s Voices and Bartok’s Monster projects.

Program:

Franz Schubert - Quartettsatz in C minor, D.703

Amy Beach - Quartet for Strings in One Movement

Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel - String Quartet in E-flat major

title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Public open hours will resume the first full week of the fall 2026 semester as follows:

Description: Praised by The New Yorker as “a fresh and vital young participant in what is a golden age of American string quartets,” the Daedalus Quartet has established itself as a leader among the new generation of string ensembles. Since winning the top prize in the Banff International String Quartet Competition, they have performed in many of the world’s leading musical venues including Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center, the Library of Congress, the Gardner Museum, and abroad at Vienna’s Musikverein, the Salzburg Mozarteum, the Concertgebouw, the Cité de la Musique in Paris, as well as in leading venues in Japan.

The Daedalus Quartet has won plaudits for its adventurous exploration of contemporary music including commissions of Fred Lerdahl’s Third String Quartet and Chaconne , Joan Tower’s White Water , Huck Hodge’s The Topography of Desire , David Horne’s Flight from the Labyrinth , and Vivian Fung’s Frenetic Memories.

Since 2006, the Daedalus Quartet has served as Quartet-in-Residence at the University of Pennsylvania where they are recognized for their innovative programming and interdisciplinary collaborations, particularly in their Beethoven Quartet cycle, Music and Migration, Hearing Women’s Voices and Bartok’s Monster projects.
