Description: How do academic cultures shape the ways we teach, learn and engage with challenging ideas?

Participants will share perspectives on innovations in teaching and learning, the growing role of generative AI in education, academic freedom and the discussion of sensitive topics in the classroom and evolving expectations of students and instructors. The conversation will also examine how institutional policies, political and social developments and educational traditions influence academic experiences, particularly for international students, faculty and scholars working in exile.

By bringing together voices from different disciplines, institutions and educational contexts, the roundtable aims to foster dialogue, exchange ideas and reflect on the challenges and opportunities shaping higher education today.

title: Colloquium with Dr. David Badre (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
Colloquium with Dr. David Badre takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Baker Hall 336B.
Event: Colloquium with Dr. David Badre
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026 at 12:30 PM
Venue: Baker Hall 336B
Organizer: Neuroscience Institute
Description: Abstract

Cognitive control allows us to think and behave flexibly based on our context and goals. Most theories of cognitive control propose a control representation that enables the same input to produce different outputs contingent on contextual factors. However, the computational features of these control representations that enable this flexible mapping remain unknown. In this talk, I will focus on the geometry of neural control representations that enable cognitive control. I will present evidence from fMRI and EEG showing how these representations are organized and change as a function of different task structures, over the course of a trial, and over the course of practice; and I will discuss how these changes relate to efficient behavioral control.

title: Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at 1:00 PM at Virtual.
Event: Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026 at 1:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Virtual
Organizer: NextManufacturing
Description: Abstract

The anisotropy of the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V additively manufactured (AM) via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) is increased by the long and textured columnar prior beta grains that typically occur despite the high cooling rates (105–107 K/s). Additionally, both AM and conventionally fabricated Ti-6Al-4V exhibit dwell-fatigue sensitivity at room-temperature, resulting in premature failure in the low-cycle fatigue regime. This work explores the design and printing of yttria dispersion-hardened Ti-6Al-4V with minimal powder feedstock preparation. A uniformly dispersed yttria with a mean particle size of∼100 nm in the Ti-6Al-4V matrix decreases the transverse size of the prior beta grains. Furthermore, STEM bright-field micrographs reveal dispersoid pinning of dislocations, and STEM EDS confirms that the dispersoids are yttria as expected. A modest increase in room-temperature microhardness is observed, and room-temperature nanoindentation creep results show a∼64% lower mean creep rate compared to standard PBF-LB Ti-6Al-4V. Additionally, a room-temperature compression test was performed to determine the respective yield strengths to study cold creep, and its implications are discussed. At normalized stresses, ODS Ti-6Al-4V exhibits substantially lower long-term creep rates, albeit with greater initial deformation. Description: Active Matter: The Physics of Self-Organization

Birds flock, bees swarm and fish school. These are just some of the remarkable examples of collective behavior found in nature. Physicists have been able to capture some of this behavior by modeling organisms as ``flying spins’’ that align with their neighbors according to simple but noisy rules. Successes like these have spawned a field devoted to the physics of active matter – matter made not of atom and molecules but of entities that consume energy to generate their own motion and forces. Through interactions, collectives of such active particles organize in emergent structures on scales much larger than that of the individuals. Living systems are the paradigm of such behavior, but same behavior has also been mimicked in the lab through the engineering a variety of ``active particles’’ that self-assemble to form smart materials.

In this lecture I will introduce the field of active matter and highlight ongoing efforts by physicists, biologists, engineers and mathematicians to model the complex behavior of these systems, with the goal of identifying universal principles. I will specifically focus on two examples of active behavior. title: Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Posner Hall 151.
Event: Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026 at 4:00 PM
Venue: Posner Hall 151
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures
Organizer: Statistics & Data Science Department
Description: Abstract : We introduce the Sinkhorn treatment effect, an entropic optimal transport measure of divergence between counterfactual distributions. Unlike classical quantities such as the average treatment effect, this measure captures differences across entire distributions. We analyze this divergence as a statistical functional and show it can be written as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings with an appropriate kernel. This characterization allows us to establish first-order pathwise differentiability in general, and second-order pathwise differentiability under the null hypothesis of equal counterfactual distributions. Leveraging this smoothness, we construct debiased estimators and use them to obtain asymptotically valid tests for distributional treatment effects with a fixed entropic regularization parameter. Because the power of the test depends on this unknown parameter, we further propose an aggregated test that combines evidence across a grid of regularization choices. Experiments on simulated and image data demonstrate the practical advantages of our estimator and testing procedure.

Bio : Alex Luedtke is a Professor of Health Care Policy and Affiliate in Statistics at Harvard University. Previously, he held faculty appointments in Statistics and Biostatistics at the University of Washington and Fred Hutch.

title: Ghostly Preferences: When Coherence Requires a Strict Preference Among Equivalent Random Variables (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
Ghostly Preferences: When Coherence Requires a Strict Preference Among Equivalent Random Variables takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at 5:00 PM at Baker Hall, Giant Eagle Auditorium (A51).
Event: Ghostly Preferences: When Coherence Requires a Strict Preference Among Equivalent Random Variables
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026 at 5:00 PM to 6:30 PM
Venue: Baker Hall, Giant Eagle Auditorium (A51)
Organizer: Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences
Description: Presenter: Teddy Seidenfeld

Abstract: When utilities for outcomes are bounded, or when all variables are simple, it is required by (canoncial) expected utility to have preferences defined over probability distributions or lotteries over outcomes. That is, under such circumstances two random variables with a common probability distribution over outcomes – equivalent random variables – must occupy the same place in an agent’s preference ordering over lotteries. For example, with outcomes determined by a flip of a fair coin (i.e, where the probability of landing heads = the probability of landing tails = 1/2), winning $1 if heads and losing $1 if tails is equally preferred to losing $1 if heads and winning $1 if tails. Also, then one is indifferent between trading one of these lotteries for the other.

Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

text:

Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 at 12:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall, 7316
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Title: The Character of PRX: Editorial Insights from the First 15 Years and Beyond

Abstract: PRX is published by the American Physical Society, a nonprofit membership society of scientists. Its mission goal is to select around 250 *landmark* papers a year from all fields of physics and showcase them to a broad and multidisciplinary readership.

After 15 years, one might still wonder exactly what PRX is—or, asked differently, how PRX defines a “landmark” through the peer-review process. As an author or referee, you may be curious about how PRX editors actually select these papers. Furthermore, there is always the fair question: are these selections always accurate?

In this talk, I will discuss how we approach these questions. Many of these questions do not have a black-and-white answer in the case of a single paper. Instead, open-minded, reasoned, and constructive dialogue among authors, editors, and referees is key. Ultimately, we, at PRX, strive to navigate the editorial and peer-review process effectively to ensure that the experience is meaningful, productive, and - at times - even a pleasure for everyone involved.

title: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University) (Tuesday, October 27, 2026)
text:
CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University) takes place on Tuesday, October 27, 2026 at 1:00 PM at Wean Hall 7218.
Event: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University)
Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 at 1:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 7218
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: An Adaptive Variational Dual Scheme for equation solving

Abstract: I will describe a scheme for converting the question of solving a given system of equations and associated side-conditions into a variational problem whose formal Euler-Lagrange system recovers the given system and side-conditions using a change-of-variables generated by the scheme. The variational principle is convex, and the method uses a string of such convex variational principles to seek a solution of the original question as an interior minimizer of the last variational problem of the string. Weak coercivity of a variational problem in the string endows its minimizer the status of a weaker `variational dual solution’ to the original, possibly non-variational problem. This last point of view is directly related to Y. Brenier’s Hidden Convexity approach to nonlinear PDE.

Due to the inherent convexity of the scheme, it allows for obtaining `unstable’ solutions of the original, primal system of equations in a `stable’ manner. A ChatGPT-enabled exploration of the scheme in the context of approximation of the mixed curvature isometric embedding problem from R^2 to R^3 will be discussed, as well as the problem of finding deformations of a membrane with prescribed principal stretch fields. This last problem is practically important for questions of sensing and actuation.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

text:

Date: Wednesday, October 28, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Rich Holman

Title: Tensor Catalyzed Scalar Decoherence in Inflation

Abstract. We provide the first complete calculation of the leading contribution to the decoherence of primordial fluctuations in the scalar part of the metric fluctuations within simplest, single-clock, inflationary models, assuming decoherence comes from gravitational interactions with an environment made up of the other, unmeasured, short-wavelength scalar and tensor modes.

We include the contributions from all of the contributing interactions at leading order in powers of (H/Mp) and of the slow-roll parameter ϵ. Unlike all extant calculations in the literature we find a result that is not slow-roll suppressed (and so is the same order of magnitude as tensor-mode decoherence). The difference arises because the dominant decoherence comes from interactions that involve both the tensor and scalar environments simultaneously (and so are missed when they are examined separately). We verify that the leading contributions to decoherence are UV finite (as they must be). We confirm that the interactions driving decoherence become time-local and Gaussian in the deep super-Hubble inflationary regime and show how this can be used to reliably compute the evolution of the purity in the late-time regime relevant for observations (where naive perturbation theory is known to break down). Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures
Organizer: Languages, Cultures & Applied Linguistics Department
Description: The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben , a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.

Category: Community Outreach, Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Center for the Arts in Society
Description: In 2015, after a violent attack on her beloved partner, Virginia Eubanks suddenly became a family caregiver. In the weeks, months, and years that followed, she and her partner struggled to stay afloat as they faced wave upon wave of setbacks, including a serious case of post-traumatic stress disorder. Then, a second case. Eubanks developed “collateral” PTSD, a condition common among caregivers but rarely discussed.

An old lifesaving manual provided unexpected help. Inspired by its lessons, Eubanks studied wilderness first aid, kayak self-rescue, winter survival, bushwhacking, and lifeguarding. She interviewed experts and everyday heroes—from neuroscientists to monks to forest rangers.
Join Eubanks to discover what it takes to build communities of care that can sustain us in uncertain times.

About the Artist:

Christopher Mark Jones draws from folk, country, blues, jazz and R&B sources to stage his literate folk-rock meditations. Using diverse points of view to narrate and critique life and love in uncertain times, he invites listeners to think, feel and dance. Recorded and live arrangements leave space for his musical co-conspirators to both express their personalities and honor the host creation. Listeners hear echoes of “Greg Brown’s pacing and a Lyle Lovett attitude” (Ben Shannon), as well as of John Prine, Bruce Coburn and Darrell Scott.

Between careers as a basketball player and French professor, Christopher busked in Paris, toured the UK, Denmark and Holland, and played New England clubs. He now tours and streams solo from Pittsburgh, PA, and plays regionally in formats varying from solo to full band. Looking for the Light (2021) is his sixth recording of original folk/roots songs, while Montréal Encore (2022) is a French-language recording created in collaboration with the poet Bernard Pozier.

Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

title: PCG Reading Group: Konstantin Tikhomirov (Thursday, October 29, 2026)
text:
PCG Reading Group: Konstantin Tikhomirov takes place on Thursday, October 29, 2026 at 10:00 AM at Wean Hall 5320.
Event: PCG Reading Group: Konstantin Tikhomirov
Date: Thursday, October 29, 2026 at 10:00 AM to 11:00 AM
Venue: Wean Hall 5320
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: On the optimal dependence on distortion in Dvoretzky’s theorem

Abstract: A seminal result of Dvoretzky-Milman asserts that every n-dimensional normed space contains an almost Euclidean subspace of at least logarithmic dimension. The exact interdependence between the subspace dimension and the distortion (i.e quantification of “almost Euclidean”) has remained unsettled for several decades. A recent AI-assisted paper of Klartag and Moshe has produced a resolution of the problem, using remarkably elementary arguments. I will present a proof of their result. If there is time left, I will talk about another recent AI-assisted breakthrough.

Description: Abstract Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. Topic: Where do stars explode in the ISM? A new constraint on stellar feedback models

Abstract: In this talk, I will present the first set of direct observational constraints on where stars explode in the interstellar medium (ISM) from high-resolution surveys of nearby galaxies with JWST, HST, VLA, ALMA and VLT/MUSE. Explosions of stars, i.e. supernovae (SNe) are the main regulators of star-formation in galaxies. They achieve this most directly by launching winds, which remove cold star-forming gas from the ISM, and creating pressure in the ISM by supplying heat, turbulence and cosmic rays. The efficiency of these processes depend sensitively on the environments where SNe occur, particularly the correlation between SNe and dense gas clouds. While there is evidence of SN shocks interacting with molecular clouds, the ionizing radiation and stellar winds from massive stars can quickly unbind and disperse dense clouds before SNe occur. How these different feedback channels limit star-formation in molecular clouds and launch winds is one of the biggest open questions in galaxy evolution. I will discuss how we can address this topic with the novel method of observations of evolved massive stars and supernova remnants in the Local Volume, supplied by high-resolution multiwavelength surveys like PHANGS, LGLBS and SDSS. From Sensing to Adaptation: Human-Centered Intelligence in the Built Environment

The built environment is increasingly able to sense, learn, and respond, creating new opportunities to rethink how we design, construct, operate, and experience buildings and infrastructure. This talk presents our research toward human-centered intelligent built environments, from multimodal sensing and modeling of human experiences and interactions with buildings to AI-enabled simulation of human behavior and emergency response, adaptive building systems, and human–robot interaction and teleoperation in construction. Across these applications, a common question drives our work: how can we move beyond systems that simply collect data or automate predefined tasks toward environments and machines that understand context, anticipate human needs, and adapt their behavior accordingly? I will discuss recent advances and remaining challenges in creating built environments in which people, machines, and physical spaces can increasingly sense, learn from, and adapt to one another.

Tuning Atomically Precise Materials for Sustainable Chemistry

Host: Stefan Bernhard

Friday, October 30th, 2026
12:30 p.m.
Mellon Institute Conference Room 348

Abstract: With the advent of nanotechnology in the mid-1980s, nanomaterials have attracted tremendous interest due to their unique properties which make them suitable for diverse applications. However, the inherent polydispersity of conventional nanoparticles has precluded an atomic-level understanding of their structure-property relationships. This, in turn, has greatly hampered the complete realization of their target functional properties in real-world applications. This talk will focus on leveraging the principles of synthetic organic and inorganic chemistry to engineer multifunctional atomically precise materials for applications in catalysis, water harvesting, and iodine capture. Specifically, we will discuss two classes of materials, (1) molecularly pure, ligand-protected coinage metal clusters, and (2) covalent organic frameworks (COFs), which are atomically precise tunable materials with extraordinary porosity and crystallinity. Overall, these efforts aim to establish design rules for making functional heterogeneous nanomaterials with known structure-property-function relationships.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Saturday, October 31, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Saturday, October 31, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

title: Guest Lecture: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation (Monday, November 2, 2026)
text:
Guest Lecture: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation takes place on Monday, November 2, 2026 at 10:00 AM at Porter Hall A7F.
Event: Guest Lecture: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation
Date: Monday, November 2, 2026 at 10:00 AM to 11:00 AM
Venue: Porter Hall A7F
Organizer: Civil and Environmental Engineering Department
Description: Title: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation

Abstract:

Digital transformation in the built environment is increasingly defined not by technology adoption alone, but by the ability to demonstrate measurable value. AI, openBIM, VDC, digital twins, Lean practices, and performance metrics are becoming more closely connected as organizations seek better project, asset, and business outcomes.

Drawing on more than 30 years of experience in openBIM and digital innovation, including owner-focused initiatives across 30 countries, Dr. Calvin Kam will explore how governments, owners, and industry organizations can translate emerging technologies, open standards, and mandates into practical implementation strategies and measurable results.

Building on his work as Founder and CEO of Strategic Building Innovation, his work with buildingSMART International on Global openBIM Mandates and openBIM Business Value, and research associated with Stanford University’s Center for Integrated Facility Engineering (CIFE), the presentation will examine how frameworks such as the VDC Scorecard can help organizations connect information requirements, quality controls, technology adoption, KPIs, and performance with broader business value.

Looking forward, the session will explore how AI, openBIM, and VDC can increasingly enable digital twins, GIS, IoT, sustainability, and decarbonization - creating a stronger foundation for informed decision-making, smarter mandates, and improved w

Bio: Praneeth Vepakomma is currently a Visiting Assistant Professor at MIT in IDSS and is an Assistant Professor at MBZUAI. He previously obtained his PhD at MIT in and works on trustworthy/responsible computation that includes a sub-focus on distributed (resource-efficient) and private computation in statistics, ML and data science at large. He has extensive industrial experience across Meta, Apple, Amazon, Motorola Solutions, Corning and several startups. His research focuses on developing algorithms for distributed computation in statistics & machine learning under constraints of privacy, & efficiency.

He won the Meta PhD research fellowship in Applied Statistics, two SERC Scholarships (for Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing) from MIT’s Schwarzman college of computing. He co-founded a research based non-profit (Integrity Distributed) that won the Financial Times Digital Innovation Award. He won a Best Student Paper Award at FL-IJCAI, a Baidu Best Paper Award at NeurIPS-SpicyFL and a Best Paper Runner Up Award at FG-2021. His technical work is inspired by foundations of non-asymptotic statistics, randomized algorithms, learning augmented algorithms, combinatorics, and at times just by systems design. He was Interviewed in the book, ‘Data Scientist: The Definitive Guide to Becoming a Data Scientist’ and has organized several workshops at ICLR

text:

Venue: Wean Hall, 7316
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Price: Free
Description: Speaker: Daniel Baxter (Fermilab)

Topic: Harnessing Quantum Sensors to Search for Dark Matter

Abstract: The CosmiQuantum group at Fermilab is at the center of understanding the relationship between particle impacts in quantum processors and qubit errors. This research hopes to enable high-fidelity quantum computation by resolving the issue of phonon-mediated correlated errors following cosmic ray impacts in a superconducting qubit chip. Additionally, this challenge for quantum computing presents a unique opportunity for fundamental science, as the same errors that follow a particle impact can be used to search for low-energy signatures of new physics originating from dark matter or neutrino impacts. At Fermilab, we have two world-class underground facilities which are already being used to study this problem: NEXUS and QUIET. I will present results from operating superconducting qubits in each of these facilities, and the potential implications towards utilizing qubits as sensors of new physics.

title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections (Tuesday, November 3, 2026)
text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Tuesday, November 3, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Date: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at 5:30 PM to 7:00 PM
Venue: Carnegie Museum of Art
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: School of Art
Description: Join us for an evening with artist Kearra Amaya Gopee as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

About the Artist

Kearra Amaya Gopee (born 1994, Miami, FL, raised in Carapichaima, Kairi (Trinidad and Tobago); lives on Lenape land in New York) is an anti-disciplinary artist and facilitator. Using video, sculpture, sound, and writing, they identify both violence and time as primary conditions that undergird the anti-Black world in which they work. Gopee has shown work at documenta 15, Kassel, Germany (2022), and The Kitchen, among other international film venues. They have participated in residencies at Skowhegan, the International Studio and Curatorial Program, Headlands Center for the Arts, and NLS Kingston. They have been awarded fellowships at MacDowell, the Leslie Lohman Museum, Queer|Art, and the Global Fund for Women. In 2024, Gopee was an Elaine G. Weitzen Fellow at the Whitney Museum Independent Study Program. They have lectured at Emory University, Rutgers University, and the Caltech-Huntington Program in Visual Culture. In 2025, Gopee was an artist in residence at MASS MoCA. They hold an MFA from University of California, Los Angeles, with a concentration in interdisciplinary studio and a BFA in photography and imaging from New York University.

Description: The Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM) at Carnegie Mellon is hosting a meeting, Formalization for Physics, organized by Sergey Cherkis, Michael Douglas, James Halverson, and Xi Yin on November 4-6. Local faculty and students are welcome to attend. Please register using the link below; you can join the participants’ discussion channel on the ICARM Zulip.

Register: https://icarm.io/join/0btzmSk86L5VdlJqNmQ7m1B6CQP6TKZ-7e1Vr-ZGYcw/

Zulip: https://icarm.zulipchat.com/join/pueyd62pbxstlmc43qeojl7q/

Description: Formal methods are becoming increasingly relevant to physics, not only as tools for checking completed arguments but also as instruments for clarifying definitions, exposing hidden assumptions, and organizing large bodies of technical knowledge. This workshop will bring together theoretical physicists, mathematical physicists, mathematicians, and proof-assistant practitioners to identify where machine-checked reasoning can be genuinely useful for physics research.

The proposal is not that formalization should replace physical intuition. The more realistic and scientifically useful goal is to understand how formalization can make precise which parts of an argument are rigorous, which parts depend on explicit mathematical assumptions, and which parts remain heuristic. This is especially relevant in theoretical and mathematical physics, where important arguments often involve several layers of definitions, conventions, and intermediate structures

Date: Friday, November 6, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

title: Graduate Student Seminar (Friday, November 6, 2026)
text:
Graduate Student Seminar takes place on Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Wean Hall (Room 7500).
Event: Graduate Student Seminar
Date: Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:30 PM
Venue: Wean Hall (Room 7500)
Organizer: Materials Science and Engineering Department
Description: Abstract: Material interfaces are critical frontiers where macroscopic functionality
emerges from microscopic phenomena—where bonds break, charges migrate, and heat carriers scatter. While first-principles molecular dynamics (FPMD) provides atomic-level insight into these processes, high computational cost has traditionally restricted its application to small systems (hundreds of atoms) and short timescales (picoseconds). I will discuss our approach for overcoming these limitations by integrating FPMD with Bayesian Inference, neural networks, and rare-event sampling. By bridging the gap between quantum fidelity and long-time and length-scale phenomena, we explore three distinct technological frontiers: (i) reactive chemistry at polymer–metal interfaces for sustainable plastic recycling, (ii) nanoscale heat transfer in alloys in the presence of grain boundaries and dopants, and (iii) charge transfer at semiconductor–water interfaces to realize robust nanoscale quantum sensors. Overall, these results show how predictive, first-principles knowledge of interfacial behavior can provide a rational design roadmap for the next generation of chemical recycling, thermal management, and quantum technologies.

text:

Event: X in the Loop Webinar Series
Date: Friday, November 6, 2026 at 9:00 PM to 10:00 PM
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures
Organizer: Languages, Cultures & Applied Linguistics Department
Description: Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

Date: Monday, November 9, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM

Organizer: Engineering and Public Policy Department
Description: Environmental justice research often examines the burden of pollution in relation to the population’s socioeconomic vulnerability. Climate justice research examines differential responsibility, asking who emits and who ultimately carries the burden they create. Urban mobility justice research rarely combines these two questions empirically, even though mobility is where they intersect most directly, since travel generates emissions and also shapes where resulting pollution concentrations fall across the city. This talk presents findings from an empirical study of Bogotá, Colombia, that measures both sides of this relationship at the level of city blocks, combining residential pollution concentration (NO2 and PM2.5) with a block-level proxy for travel-emission responsibility built from official mobility and emissions data. Two findings challenge a simple story in which the poor pollute least and suffer most. First, pollution concentration does not increase monotonically with deprivation; it peaks at intermediate socioeconomic levels. Second, emission responsibility does decline cleanly with vulnerability, but the resulting imbalance, where responsibility is low and pollution concentration is high, concentrates in population segments that can only be identified by combining policy instruments that separately inform socioeconomic vulnerability and the spatial distribution of the imbalance. text:

Event: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)
Date: Monday, November 9, 2026 at 3:30 PM

Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Price: Free
Description: Speaker: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)

Topic: Arch and Scaffold: Jordan’s statistical transformation theory and von Neumann’s Hilbert space formalism

Abstract: In early 1927, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, independently of one another, published their versions of a general formalism tying the various forms of the new quantum theory together and giving the theory’s statistical interpretation in full generality. This formalism has come to be known as the Dirac-Jordan (statistical) transformation theory. A few months later, in response to these publications, John von Neumann published his Hilbert space formalism for quantum mechanics. The relation between these two formalisms can be captured in terms of a metaphor for theory change in which one theory serves as the scaffold for the arch of another theory. What is unclear in this case is which formalism serves as the scaffold and which one as the arch. Did von Neumann build an arch on the scaffold built by Jordan? Or did von Neumann build a scaffold to prevent the arch built by Jordan from collapsing? Either way, the arch-and-scaffold metaphor is a promising alternative to Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm shifts for understanding theory change.

Note: Based on joint work with Anthony Duncan (University of Pittsburgh)

Description: Global Entrepreneurship Week (GEW) is a global movement that celebrates and supports entrepreneurship by creating opportunities for people to learn, connect, share ideas, and take action. At Carnegie Mellon University Africa (CMU-Africa), GEW provides an opportunity to bring together students, founders, alumni, industry, investors, ecosystem partners, and the wider university community around entrepreneurship, innovation, and technology. Through the Innovation Hub, CMU-Africa supports students and entrepreneurs through business incubation, mentorship, technical talent, industry connections, and opportunities to develop and test solutions to real-world challenges. GEW 2026 will build on these efforts by creating a week that brings the CMU-Africa entrepreneurship community together to explore ideas, build capabilities, connect with opportunities, and showcase what is being created.

This year’s theme “Entrepreneurs Thrive Here” reflects CMU-Africa’s ambition to create an environment where students and founders can explore entrepreneurship, develop their ideas, access the resources and networks they need, and turn ideas into meaningful solutions. It recognises that entrepreneurs thrive when they have access not only to knowledge and technology, but also to people, mentorship, opportunities, and a supportive community.

Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

text:

Event: CMU Theory Seminar: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)

Venue: Wean Hall, 8327
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Physics Department
Description: Speaker: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)

Title: Exploring non-equilibrium universality with Schwinger–Keldysh effective field theories

Abstract: Dissipation and noise arise throughout physics, from condensed matter to cosmology, whenever observable degrees of freedom interact with a medium. The Schwinger–Keldysh formalism provides a systematic framework for describing such dynamics. Building on techniques developed in fluctuating hydrodynamics, I will discuss how symmetry, locality and unitarity constrain the allowed interactions. I will then explain how dissipation and noise modify the EFT power counting compared with vacuum quantum field theory. Using a scalar theory with a Kardar–Parisi–Zhang interaction, I will finally explore the emergence of a non-equilibrium universality class and discuss whether cosmological expansion in de Sitter spacetime can make this new dynamical regime accessible in three spatial dimension.

title: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Iain Cheeseman (Wednesday, November 11, 2026)
text:
Departmental Seminar: Dr. Iain Cheeseman takes place on Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room.
Event: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Iain Cheeseman
Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 1:40 PM
Venue: Mellon Institute (MCS), 348 Conference Room
Organizer: Biological Sciences Department
Description: Guest Speaker: Iain Cheeseman, PhD

Professor of Biology at MIT

Core Member, Whitehead Institute

Title: “Unlocking the Hidden Proteome”

Our lab is fascinated by the molecular machinery that directs core cellular processes, and in particular how these processes are modulated and rewired across different physiological contexts. Our work has focused on the proteins that direct chromosome segregation and cell division, including the macromolecular kinetochore structure that mediates chromosome-microtubule interactions. Although cell division is an essential cellular process, this machinery is remarkably flexible in its composition and properties, which can vary dramatically between species and are even modulated within the same organism — over the cell cycle, during development, and across diverse physiological situations. To define the basis by which the kinetochore and other core cellular structures are rewired to adapt to diverse situations and functional requirements, we are currently investigating diverse transcriptional, translational, and post-translational mechanisms that act to generate proteomic variability both within individual cells and across tissues, cell state, development, and disease.

title: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen (Wednesday, November 11, 2026)
text:
ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen takes place on Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Posner Hall Grand Room (POS 340).
Event: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen
Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:30 PM
Venue: Posner Hall Grand Room (POS 340)
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures
Organizer: Languages, Cultures & Applied Linguistics Department
Description: Translingual Borders: Refugee Testimony and the Politics of Translation

Isabelle Chen , assistant professor of global French studies, will challenge the assumption that translation is a liberatory practice — one that enables people to cross linguistic, cultural and geographic borders — by examining how translation can also reinforce borders, reproduce unequal power dynamics and constrain individual agency.

Focusing on Shumona Sinha’s novel Assommons les pauvres ! ( Down with the Poor! ), Dr. Chen’s talk explores the experiences of a Bengali interpreter working with asylum seekers in France. She examines how Sinha uses translation both as a literary strategy and a central thematic motif to portray interpretation as a potential barrier to human mobility and freedom.

Drawing on translation theory and recent migration data, Dr. Chen considers what literary representations of translation can reveal about its real-world consequences — and about the roles of multilingualism, interpretation and language in immigration policy and advocacy today.

title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University) (Thursday, November 12, 2026)
text:
ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University) takes place on Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Wean Hall 8220.
Event: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
Date: Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 3:00 PM to 4:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 8220
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Speaker: Veit Elser , Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

Description: Please join us for CMU Engineering’s virtual program, “Faculty Insights: A 20 Minute Briefing.” In this series, faculty will share insights into their research, its impact, and provide perspective for the future of the field. Following the presentation, attendees will have an opportunity to direct questions and comments to the speaker.

“Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions”

Rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers could substantially increase U.S. power sector emissions and electricity costs by 2030, with particularly large impacts in regions such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Using a detailed energy model covering 26 interconnected U.S. power regions, we evaluate how demand growth, fuel prices, and federal policies affect electricity generation, infrastructure investment, and costs. Data centers could push U.S. power sector carbon emissions up by as much as 28% and spike regional electricity costs by up to 57% by 2030.

Join Café con Libros for a conversation celebrating the release of The City-Women , the debut play by playwright, actor, and musician Mallorie Sievert .

Set in a 17th-century cloistered convent in Latin America, The City-Women is a sapphic historical romance that follows four Latine women navigating faith, identity, and love within a strict religious environment. Mallorie will be joined by director, playwright, and longtime collaborator Sara LiBrandi for a discussion exploring the intersections of feminism, queerness, Christianity, and Latinidad, followed by an audience Q&A and book signing.

About the Author

Mallorie Sievert (she/her) is a Latina playwright, actor, and musician based in New York City. She graduated from Elon University in 2024, and The City-Women is her debut play. Her acting credits include Shucked (Broadway First National Tour) and Heartbreak Hotel (Engeman Theater).

Date: Friday, November 13, 2026 at 12:30 PM
Venue: Wean Hall (Room 7500)
Organizer: Materials Science and Engineering Department
Description: Abstract: Advances in thin film growth techniques, which allow for the precise layer-by-layer growth of epitaxial materials, have opened the door to discoveries not previously achievable through bulk synthesis. Pertinent examples include emergent phenomena at oxide heterointerfaces such as two-dimensional electron gases, interfacial superconductivity and novel magnetic properties. In this presentation, I will discuss our use of first principles calculations to explore how the character of heterostructure interfaces can be used to influence material stability and functionality. I will illustrate the role that charge transfer plays in driving magnetism and anomalous dielectric responses at oxide interfaces, and how these can be modulated through chemical identity and interface disorder. Collectively, these results demonstrate unprecedented control over interfacial charge and spin, creating a new avenue for a wide range of applications such as in oxide electronics.

Dr. Valentino R. Cooper is a Distinguished R&D Staff Member and Section Head for Foundational and Quantum Materials Science in the Materials Sciences and Technology Division at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. He serves as Director of the Department of Energy-funded Energy Frontier Research Center on Fast and Cooperative Ion Transport in Polymer Electrolytes (FaCT). Date: Saturday, November 14, 2026

Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

title: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress (Monday, November 16, 2026)
text:
Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress takes place on Monday, November 16, 2026 at 9:30 AM at CUC – Danforth Conference Room.
Event: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress
Date: Monday, November 16, 2026 at 9:30 AM to 11:00 AM
Venue: CUC – Danforth Conference Room
Category: Career & Professional Development, Health & Wellness, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Office of the Vice Provost for Faculty
Description: This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

Bio: Adam Smith is a Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at Boston University. His research interests lie in data privacy and cryptography, and their connections to machine learning, statistics, information theory, and quantum computing. He obtained his Ph.D. from MIT in 2004 and has held visiting positions at the Weizmann Institute of Science, UCLA, and Harvard. He previously was a Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at Penn State. He received a Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE) in 2009; a 2016 Theory of Cryptography Test of Time award; the 2019 Eurocrypt Test of Time award; and the 2017 Gödel Prize.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Tuesday, November 17, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Tuesday, November 17, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

title: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford) (Tuesday, November 17, 2026)
text:
CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford) takes place on Tuesday, November 17, 2026 at 2:00 PM at Wean Hall 7218.
Event: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford)
Date: Tuesday, November 17, 2026 at 2:00 PM to 3:00 PM
Venue: Wean Hall 7218
Category: Conferences, Panels & Lectures, Open to the Public
Organizer: Mathematical Sciences Department
Description: Please note the unusual time.

Quantitative estimates for almost harmonic maps

Abstract: A fundamental question in the analysis of variational problems is whether functions that almost minimise a given energy, or almost solve its Euler-Lagrange equations, provide good approximations of true minimisers or critical points. In practice, one would like to understand this question not only at a qualitative level, but to obtain precise quantitative control on the distance of almost solutions to exact solutions in terms of the size of the error.

A major challenge in such a quantitative analysis of geometric variational problems is that the classical approach breaks down in the presence of singularities or changes of topology.

In this talk, we will discuss these issues for the Dirichlet energy of maps from surfaces into Riemannian manifolds for which the concentration of energy on small domains leads to a loss of compactness and the formation of a so-called bubble tree.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Thursday, November 19, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Thursday, November 19, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Description: Co-creating tomorrow: Community Driven Engineering for a Resilient Future” is a webinar series exploring the critical intersection of community wisdom and engineering expertise in the face of a changing climate. Organized by CERCA, CMU CEE’s Center for Engineering Resilience and Climate Adaptation, this series will foster a deeper understanding of how community engagement can enhance the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of climate adaptation initiatives. text:

Event: Graduate Student Seminar
Date: Friday, November 20, 2026 at 12:30 PM
Venue: Wean Hall (Room 7500)
Organizer: Materials Science and Engineering Department
Description: Abstract: The design, discovery, characterization and control of novel materials is perhaps the most important research area for humanity as it moves into the 21rst century. A myriad of societal problems concerning energy, clean water and air, and medicine all need to be solved by the discovery of new compounds with dramatically improved, or even new, properties. The search for such materials requires a blending of skills and mindsets that, traditionally, have been segregated into different academic disciplines: physics, chemistry, metallurgy, materials science. In this colloquium I will outline the basic philosophy and techniques that we use to search for novel materials. These include a combination of intuition, experience, compulsive optimism and a desire to share discovery.[1]

In the second half of the lecture, the specific case of superconductivity will be used as an example of one such search. Over the past couple of decades a growing sense of where and even how to search for new superconductors has been developing, with the recent discoveries of MgB2 and the FeAs based materials providing, at least for me, clear guidance. [2]

[1] Paul C. Canfield, Rep. Prog. Phys. 83 [2020] 016501.

[2]Paul C. Canfield, Nature Materials 10 [2011] 259.

Date: Saturday, November 21, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

text:
CyLab Seminar: Andrew Ilyas takes place on Monday, November 30, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Zoom and CIC 4501, Panther Hollow Conference Room.
Event: CyLab Seminar: Andrew Ilyas
Date: Monday, November 30, 2026 at 12:00 PM
Venue: Zoom and CIC 4501, Panther Hollow Conference Room
Organizer: CyLab
Description: Speaker: Andrew Ilyas
Assistant Professor, Electrical and Computer Engineering & Software and Societal Systems
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Talk title coming soon

Abstract: Abstract coming soon

Bio:

Andrew Ilyas is an assistant professor at CMU. Previously, he was a Stein Fellow at Stanford Statistics and a Ph.D. student MIT, where he was fortunate to be advised by Costis DaskalakisOpens in new window and Aleksander MadryOpens in new window and supported by an Open Philanthropy AI FellowshipOpens in new window. Ilyas attended MIT for undergrad, majoring in CS and in Math. Outside of research, I enjoy playing soccer and table tennis.

Ilyas’s goal is to uncover general principles that describe and predict the behavior of ML systems—ideally enabling predictably reliable future systems. This goal entails combining statistical tools with large-scale experiments to precisely understand the ML “pipeline,” from training data (and the way we collect it), to learning algorithms, to deployment. He also likes thinking broadly about (human) trust in AI systems.

title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections (Tuesday, December 1, 2026)
text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Tuesday, December 1, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Tuesday, December 1, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. (Reading Room & Exhibitions)

Description: Guest Speaker: Joshua Weinstein, PhD

Assistant Professor of Medicine

University of Chicago

Title: TBA

Joshua Weinstein is a biophysicist and molecular technologist. He works on developing DNA-based technologies for high-throughput encoding and decoding of biological information with a view toward applications in biology and medicine. He has previously worked on applying massively parallel DNA sequencing to the study of immune receptor repertoires. Recently, he invented DNA microscopy, an imaging modality that uses DNA rather than light as an imaging medium in order to generate detailed pictures of how genetic diversity distributes spatially across biological specimens.

Departmental Host: Professor Kaplow

text:
CERCA Webinar with Orange Country Water District takes place on Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Virtual - Register Below.
Event: CERCA Webinar with Orange Country Water District
Date: Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 3:30 PM to 4:30 PM
Venue: Virtual - Register Below
Organizer: Civil and Environmental Engineering Department
Description: “Co-creating tomorrow: Community Driven Engineering for a Resilient Future” is a webinar series exploring the critical intersection of community wisdom and engineering expertise in the face of a changing climate. Organized by CERCA, CMU CEE’s Center for Engineering Resilience and Climate Adaptation, this series will foster a deeper understanding of how community engagement can enhance the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of climate adaptation initiatives.

The Orange County Water District (OCWD) manages the Orange County Groundwater Basin, which provides approximately 85% of the water supply for 2.5 million people. Maintaining a reliable groundwater supply in a highly urbanized coastal basin requires an integrated approach that includes seawater intrusion protection, water reuse, stormwater capture, and managed aquifer recharge (MAR).

Seawater intrusion has been a challenge in the Orange County Groundwater Basin since the 1920s. In response, OCWD constructed the Talbert Seawater Intrusion Barrier in the 1970s, creating a hydraulic barrier to protect the basin from further seawater intrusion. Today, OCWD continues to operate and improve its coastal barriers and is evaluating development of a new barrier in the Sunset Gap to address an additional potential pathway for seawater intrusion. Bill Leever, OCWD Principal Hydrogeologist, will discuss the history, operation, and future of OCWD’s seawater intrusion barrier program.

Description: Abstract: The Mei Research Group at Zhejiang University bridges fundamental discovery and real-world innovation by integrating chemistry, materials science, engineering and medicine. We develop organic semiconductors and conductors with transformative potential for printed electronics, bioelectronics, and living electronics, pursuing both technological impact and fundamental scientific frontiers.

In this seminar, I will highlight two complementary research directions: Electrochromic Technologies and Living Electronics. Both are rooted in the precise control of light, color, ions, and electrons, yet extend these principles toward very different applications. Through Ambilight Inc., our discoveries in flexible electrochromic thin films have been translated into roll-to-roll manufacturing and commercialized for applications ranging from electric vehicles to consumer electronics. These examples illustrate how fundamental discoveries made in an academic laboratory can evolve into market-ready technologies.

Our second direction, Living Electronics, asks a more fundamental question: Can electronics become part of living systems rather than being implanted into them? Inspired by biological vision, our work on Organic Eyes seeks to emulate the sensing and processing functions of the human visual system. text:
Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections takes place on Sunday, December 6, 2026 at Posner Center.
Event: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
Date: Sunday, December 6, 2026
Venue: Posner Center
Category: Arts & Performance, Campus Life, Open to the Public
Organizer: Libraries
Description: The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only . Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

title: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress (Friday, December 11, 2026)
text:
Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress takes place on Friday, December 11, 2026 at 10:00 AM at CUC – Danforth Conference Room.
Event: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress
Date: Friday, December 11, 2026 at 10:00 AM to 11:30 AM
Venue: CUC – Danforth Conference Room
Category: Career & Professional Development, Health & Wellness, Training & Workshops
Organizer: Office of the Vice Provost for Faculty
Description: This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).
